portfolio.notes_html:
• Universe. All 6,980 equity lines in Vanguard’s full holdings file for 2026-09-30: ordinary shares, REITs, preferred shares, depositary receipts and foreign shares. Cash, FX, futures, swaps and rights are excluded.
  • Prices. Latest available session from Yahoo Finance’s quote endpoint, captured 2026-11-03 22:48 UTC. Markets close at different times; Japan was closed on 2026-11-03, for example, so its lines show the previous session. The move is in the stock’s local currency.
  • Coverage. 6,715 of 6,980 lines have a quote (96.12% of the fund, 99.76% of equity weight). The 265 unpriced lines are 0.24% of the fund and are mostly small caps in India (75), Malaysia (53), Philippines (30), United Arab Emirates (21), Singapore (17), Saudi Arabia (17), Chile (9), Taiwan (6). Every line is kept, including those below 0.001%.
  • Market cap. Yahoo market cap converted to USD using Yahoo FX pairs. Large ≥ $10B, Mid $2–$10B, Small < $2B. Unknown means the quote did not carry a market cap or an FX rate.
  • Holdings changes. The holdings file is re-fetched on every build. New lines are resolved automatically; removed lines are dropped from the quote set. The symbol and Hong Kong country caches are additive and keyed by SEDOL, so a returning line keeps its old mapping.
  • Symbol matching. Yahoo symbols are checked against the issuer name and, where available, a market-cap plausibility test. An ambiguous match is left as “—” rather than quoted under the wrong ticker.
  • Region. FTSE region from Vanguard’s country allocation. Hong Kong-listed lines are reassigned to the issuer’s country (China, Hong Kong, etc.) using Yahoo Finance profile data, so mainland Chinese issuers listed in Hong Kong sit under China rather than Pacific.
  • Sector. ICB industry as supplied by Vanguard. ICB puts some names in different buckets than GICS — payment networks, for example, sit in Industrials, and Samsung Electronics sits in Telecommunications.
  • Weights. Fund weights as reported by Vanguard; they sum to 96.35% because the rest of the fund is cash and derivatives. They are not position sizes in any particular portfolio. Vanguard’s published region and sector charts cover the whole fund, so their percentages are slightly higher than the equity-only weights here.
  • Not advice. A one-day move is noise more often than signal. This report describes the portfolio; it does not say what to do with it.

methodology_html:
Methodology

How vallmon computes its numbers, and what each one does and does not mean.

Rolling Variance Delta

The Rolling Variance Delta measures how far current realized volatility has expanded or compressed relative to its immediate historical baseline:

delta_sigma = sigma_current / mu_sigma(t - N)
  1. Daily log returns: r_t = ln(P_t / P_{t-1})
  2. Current volatility: sigma_t = stdev(r_{t-W+1 .. t}) * sqrt(252) - annualized realized volatility over W = 20 trading days (sample standard deviation, i.e. the n-1 denominator).
  3. Baseline: mu = mean(sigma_{t-N .. t-1}) - the trailing mean of the volatility profile over N = min(90, available) days (adaptive; grows into a full 90-day baseline as history accrues).
  4. Reading: delta_sigma = sigma_t / mu - a value above 1 means volatility is expanding, below 1 means it is compressing.

Volatility labels

delta_sigma Label
>= 1.5 elevated
1.15 - 1.5 expanding
0.85 - 1.15 normal
0.7 - 0.85 compressing
< 0.7 compressed

The labels describe the size of recent moves, not their direction: a steady climb in small daily steps is "compressing", just as a steady fall in small steps is. They are derived context, not a recorded signal - nothing acts on them, so re-rendering history under changed bands is acceptable (unlike the switch state, which is stored).

They are also sticky: a band must hold for VOLATILITY_CONFIRM readings (3) before the label moves. delta_sigma crosses a band edge on ordinary noise, and without that rule a single quiet session re-labels the series and implies a change in conditions that did not happen. Consequence: after a genuine turn the label lags the raw value by up to two readings.

Volatility term structure

The same realized-vol calculation is also evaluated over several windows - W ∈ {10, 20, 30, 60} trading days - to show the shape of the volatility curve. W = 20 remains the primary window for Δσ; the other legs are supplementary.

The headline term-structure signal is the slope:

slope = sigma_10 / sigma_30
  • > 1.05 -> backwardated: short-term vol sits above longer-term vol, the classic stress shape (short-dated uncertainty priced above the trend).
  • 0.95 - 1.05 -> flat: the curve is broadly level.
  • < 0.95 -> contango: short-term vol is below longer-term vol, the calm shape (recent markets quieter than the trailing window).

A window only produces a value once that many trading days of returns exist, so the longer legs (30d, 60d) appear as an em dash until enough history accrues - the same adaptive behavior as the baseline.

Drawdown switch

delta_sigma measures dispersion, not direction, so it cannot tell you whether to sell. The drawdown rule answers a narrower question that is answerable - which asset to sell from:

drawdown = close / peak - 1        peak = max close over the trailing 756d

The switch is a two-boundary state machine rather than a single threshold. The state carries forward from the previous reading:

State Entered when Signal
cash drawdown at or below -15% draw from cash
equity drawdown at or above -5% refill
unchanged anything in between hold

The band exists because a single threshold is crossed roughly three times a year on long history, which is not a state a spending decision can follow; the 15% -> 5% gap is the hysteresis that keeps it stable. A new high (drawdown 0) is inside the re-arm band, so it also returns the switch to equity.

Unlike delta-sigma this has no baseline, no fitted parameters and no forecast: it is an observable state of the price series, so it cannot drift the way a rolling statistic can. python vallmon.py drawdown prints the recent series and the current state; --annual-spend additionally translates the current cash episode into the number of months and amount of spending it covers.

The state is recorded, not derived: each reading stores the mode it was written with, and the report reads that back. Re-parameterising the thresholds therefore changes future signals only - it cannot rewrite the history of what the monitor actually said. rebuild preserves the recorded state for the same reason; pass --reset-switch if you deliberately want it re-derived under the current thresholds.

python vallmon.py backtest VT --years 20 replays the same rule over any long-history Yahoo symbol and summarises the cash episodes it would have produced. It is read-only and never touches the ticker's CSV. Recorded runs across global, regional and long-history proxies are in Backtests.

The peak window is ~3 years, so until that much history exists the rule is running on a partial window - the report states how many readings it has seen. The window and both thresholds are provisional defaults (three years, 15%, 5%), not calibrated parameters; treat a signal as information rather than a validated trigger.

Data & caveats

  • Source: Yahoo Finance VALL.L daily closes (GBP). Rows with a null close or zero volume (new-listing placeholders) are dropped, and several bars for one session are collapsed to the last close with summed volume. That collapse is a backstop: Yahoo serves range=max at hourly granularity for this ticker (observed 2026-10), which would silently turn the daily returns series into an intraday one. The fetch therefore checks the declared granularity and retries with a bounded range (range=20y) that it does serve daily.
  • Volume: each row also records that day's traded volume in ETF units (Yahoo's volume field) as context for the reading. It is not part of the Δσ metric, and it is a unit count, not a cash amount - turnover is roughly volume × close. Rows written before the column existed are backfilled from source the next time run/rebuild executes.
  • Currency: VALL.L trades in GBP, so delta_sigma includes some GBP/USD FX noise on top of pure equity volatility.
  • Short history: VALL's share class incepted on 18 Aug 2026, so early readings use a reduced baseline until ~90 trading days accumulate (~Feb 2027); the 60-day term-structure leg stays empty until ~mid-November 2026.
  • Switch state: each row also stores the mode (equity or cash) that was signalled when it was written. It is a record, not a metric: it is never drift-checked, because recomputing it under new thresholds would rewrite the signal history. Rows written before the column existed are backfilled once, from a recompute under the current thresholds, the next time run or rebuild executes. A partially-recorded series (some rows with a state, some without) warns and falls back to a recompute rather than mixing the two.
  • Reproducibility: each row is written once and never silently rewritten. If Yahoo later revises a historical close, run prints a drift warning (checked against the primary σ, baseline, Δσ and every term-structure leg); --strict makes that warning fatal so CI cannot commit a drifted series, and python vallmon.py rebuild recomputes the whole series from source. tests/test_vallmon.py additionally re-derives every committed reading from its own close column, so a series built from a different price source fails the test suite rather than quietly producing readings.
  • Partial bars: a bar captured before the 16:30 London close is incomplete, so fetch_prices drops the current session and the next run picks it up. The scheduled 18:00 UTC run is safely after the close. rebuild is consequently time-of-day dependent: running it at 14:00 and at 18:00 on the same day produces different CSVs, by design.
backtests_html:
Backtests

python vallmon.py backtest <symbol> --years <n> replays the drawdown switch over any Yahoo close series. It is read-only: nothing is written to the ticker's CSV. This page records the runs used to sanity-check the rule, not a promise about future returns.

Method

The replayed rule is exactly the live one:

  • peak = highest close over the trailing 756 trading days (~3 years);
  • switch to cash at or below -15% of that peak;
  • return to equity at or above -5%;
  • the state carries forward in between (the 15% -> 5% gap is the hysteresis).

Each run fetches daily closes for the requested window, drops today's bar, and reports the series' max drawdown, the share of readings spent in cash, the switch count, and every cash episode.

The thresholds are provisional defaults, not fitted parameters. These runs illustrate how the rule behaves; they do not select the thresholds. --sweep replays one series across nearby enter/exit pairs (reporting the worst episode length) if you want to see how sensitive the result is.

What it does not model

  • Total return. Yahoo's close is split-adjusted but not dividend-adjusted. For distributing funds (VWRL.L, VUSA.L, ISF.L, VT, SPY) dividends are missing, so drawdowns are slightly overstated and recoveries slightly understated. Accumulating share classes (VWRP.L, VWCE.DE, IWDA.L) have no distribution to lose, so their close is close to the total-return series.
  • Currency. Each series is in its own listing currency (GBP for the .L lines, EUR for VWCE.DE, USD for the US lines). No FX conversion is applied; VALL.L itself is GBP.
  • Spending and refills. The backtest reports which asset the switch would use, not a portfolio simulation. It does not model selling, refilling the cash bucket, taxes, or dealing costs.
  • Survivorship. Only series still available on Yahoo are tested; funds that closed are absent.
  • The rolling peak. The peak is a rolling ~3-year high, so an old high eventually rolls out of the window. In a long decline that both re-arms the switch earlier and keeps it in cash while the price sits below a rolling peak - see the 2000-04 Nasdaq episode.
  • Window length. The requested window changes the answer. VT fetched over 18 years (starting in late 2008, after the pre-crash peak) shows -34.5% max drawdown and a 1.72 year worst episode; over 20 years, which includes the whole 2008 decline, it shows -50.6% and 2.13 years. Compare runs only over the same window.
  • Partial peak window. Every run uses a rolling 756-close peak, so an episode that begins in the first 756 bars of a series is measured against a peak that is still forming. That understates the peak, which delays the -15% entry and makes the entry drawdown look shallower than the rule would have produced with a full window. This is not limited to the young 2019 funds: it also covers the GFC entries for VT, SPY, QQQ, VWO and ISF.L, the 2011 episodes for IWDA.L, VWCE.DE's 2022 episode, the 1992-94 episodes for ^FTSE, and the 1992 episode for ^IXIC. The 35-year indices are the only runs where the 2000-02 and 2008 episodes are measured on a full window. Affected runs and episodes are marked † below.
  • Short series. VWRP.L and VWCE.DE only start in 2019, so they contain no GFC or dot-com episode at all, on top of the partial-window effect above.

The S&P 500's longest episodes are 1937-05-13 → 1943-04-29 (5.92y, -16.2% to -5.2%) and 1929-10-23 → 1935-08-09 (5.72y, -16.5% to -5.8%). The Nasdaq's remains 2000-04-03 → 2004-11-10 (4.60y); its 1973-03-22 → 1976-11-30 episode runs 3.71y. The FTSE is unchanged at 3.96y (2001-2005) because Yahoo's series starts in 1984.

So the 4.6-year modern-era bound is a floor for severe bears, not a ceiling: a depression-style tail needs roughly six years of spending. The 1929 and 1973 entries are flagged partial-window, but unlike VT's 2008 entry the relevant peak sits inside the fetched window, so those entries are not distorted; the 1937 episode is full-window. The pre-1950 ^GSPC stretch comes from older, less clean Yahoo data, though the bar count (~252/year) suggests complete daily data.

After the dot-com peak the switch stays in cash for 4.6 years. That is not a bug: the rolling peak falls, but not fast enough - the price stays more than 15% below it until late 2004, so the -5% re-arm is never met.

What the runs show

  • Signals cluster on real corrections, not on ordinary noise: COVID (2020), the 2022 rate shock, the April 2025 sell-off, the GFC and the dot-com bust. The VWRP.L proxy produced only two episodes in 7.3 years.
  • The cash bucket needs to cover multiple years. The worst episodes are 4.60 years (^IXIC), 3.96 (^FTSE), 3.68 (^GSPC), 3.37 (VWO) and 3.27 (SPY). A one- or two-year cash reserve would have run out in 2000-04 and 2008-2011. The full-window index runs confirm the order of magnitude: ^GSPC spends 3.27 years in cash through the GFC and ^FTSE 3.06. On full history the S&P 500 needs 5.92 years (1937-43), so treat 4.6 years as a floor (see Max history).
  • Secular bears keep it in cash for a long time. VWO spends 73.8% of the period in cash, ^FTSE 33.9%, VT 36.4%. VWO's eight episodes include 2008-2011 (3.37y), 2011-2014 (2.99y), 2015-2017 (2.14y), 2018-2020 (2.44y) and 2021-2025 (3.37y). The rule is not a dip-buyer; it waits for a recovery to within 5% of a rolling 3-year peak, which in a long sideways market can take years.
  • The near proxy is too young to be reassuring. VWRP.L only starts in 2019, so it says nothing about 2000-02 or 2008; the global and index runs are what cover those.
  • The thresholds remain unvalidated. The runs show the mechanism behaves as described; they do not show that 15%/5% is the best pair. --sweep on VT or ^IXIC is the next check if the thresholds are up for debate.

Reproduce

# GBP/EUR proxies and funds
for sym in VWRP.L VWRL.L VWCE.DE IWDA.L VUSA.L ISF.L VT SPY QQQ VWO; do
  python vallmon.py backtest "$sym" --years 20
done

# 35-year price indices (quote the ^ so the shell leaves it alone)
for sym in '^GSPC' '^FTSE' '^IXIC'; do
  python vallmon.py backtest "$sym" --years 35
done

# full history, whatever Yahoo holds (can reach 1927 for ^GSPC)
for sym in '^GSPC' '^FTSE' '^IXIC'; do
  python vallmon.py backtest "$sym" --years 200
done

Results are point-in-time: Yahoo revises history and the trailing window moves, so a run today will not match this page exactly.
